definition.text: The study of how psychological factors shape the decisions of people and institutions, and how those decisions differ from what traditional economic theory predicts.

facts.text: Its main concern is the limits on how rational people's economic choices really are.
It studies where the standard assumptions that people are rational and selfish break down, looking at biases, tendencies and mental shortcuts.
It helps judge whether people choose well and whether they could be helped to choose better.
Its models combine psychology, neuroscience and microeconomic theory.
It became a distinct field in the 1970s and 1980s, though ideas such as loss aversion appear as early as Adam Smith's Theory of Moral Sentiments.
In the early 1900s economists pushed psychology out of economics and modelled people as purely rational, self-interested decision makers.
The field spread widely after Kahneman and Tversky's work, through the 1990s and 2000s.
Nobel prizes went to Herbert Simon in 1978, Daniel Kahneman and Vernon Smith in 2002, and Richard Thaler in 2017.

title: Bounded rationality

definition.text: The idea that people's rationality is limited when they decide, so they pick an option that is good enough rather than the best one.

facts.text: The limits are how hard the problem is, what the mind can work out, and how much time is available.
People therefore act as satisficers and do not carry out a full cost-benefit analysis; they take an option that meets their standard of adequacy.
Herbert A. Simon coined the term as an alternative to modelling decision-makers as perfectly rational.
Simon compared rationality to a pair of scissors: one blade is human cognitive limits, the other the structure of the environment.
Simon argued that decision-makers use heuristics, or rules of thumb, instead of strict optimisation because situations are complex.
Gerd Gigerenzer showed that simple heuristics often give better decisions than theoretically optimal procedures.
Nudges are designed to help people get around the limits and biases that bounded rationality creates.
Kahneman and Tversky's work on heuristics, risky choice and framing extended Simon's ideas into a map of bounded rationality.

contested_note: Bounded rationality remains debated across economics, psychology, law, philosophy and cognitive science.

definition.text: Two companions of bounded rationality: people have limited self-control over long-term plans, and their concern for others is real but limited.

facts.text: Bounded willpower helps explain procrastination, impulsive spending and unhealthy lifestyle choices.
Bounded willpower is closely linked to hyperbolic discounting, the tendency to value immediate rewards more than future ones.
Bounded selfishness means people also care about fairness, reciprocity and others' well-being, which helps explain charitable giving, cooperation and social norms.

title: Nudge

definition.text: A change in how choices are presented, designed to steer people's decisions without restricting their freedom to choose.

facts.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularised the idea in their 2008 book Nudge.
Nudges can simplify complex decisions by presenting information clearly, reducing mental effort.
Making organ donation the default with an opt-out has, alongside other policies, raised actual donation rates.
Showing calorie counts on menus is a nudge that supplies missing information for healthier choices.
Critics say nudges can be manipulative, diminish autonomy or lack scientific credibility; Sunstein has defended them at length.
A 2024 review reported that fewer than half of nudging experiments keep a long-term effect when re-tested.

contested_note: Critics charge that nudges are manipulative or scientifically weak, and defenders such as Sunstein dispute these charges.
notes: Nudge theory has its own crawled page owned by another chapter; this entry uses the Behavioral economics section and may fold into it.

definition.text: The study of how psychology influences the behaviour of investors and financial analysts.

facts.text: It assumes investors are not always rational, have limited self-control and are swayed by biases.
Its central question is why market participants make systematic errors, which affect prices and returns and make markets inefficient.

definition.text: The study of strategic decisions between people using game theory together with experiments from economics and psychology.

facts.text: Colin Camerer invented it.
Its experiments test departures from standard theory, such as the neglect of altruism, fairness and framing effects.
It has been applied to interactive learning and social preferences.

definition.text: The use of controlled experiments, analysed with statistical and computational tools, to study economic questions.

facts.text: Experimental data are used to estimate effect sizes, test economic theories and shed light on how markets work.
Experiments usually pay subjects in cash to mimic real-world incentives.
Vernon L. Smith shared the 2002 Nobel prize for establishing laboratory experiments as a tool of economic analysis.
Prominent behavioural and experimental economists tend to share techniques, though some see a schism between the two fields.

definition.text: An interdisciplinary field that explains how people make decisions by combining neuroscience with economics and psychology.

facts.text: It asks both how economic behaviour informs our understanding of the brain and how brain research can constrain economic models.

title: Criticism of behavioral economics

definition.text: The debate over whether behavioural findings undermine standard economic analysis and whether they hold up outside the laboratory.

facts.text: Papers by Armen Alchian in 1950 and Gary Becker in 1962 argued that standard neoclassical analysis works even without assuming fully rational individuals.
Many behavioural studies fail to reproduce when repeated, part of the replicability crisis.
Behavioural economists responded by turning from lab experiments to field studies.
Matthew Rabin counters that results tend to be consistent across many situations and places.

contested_note: Critics question the replicability and real-world validity of behavioural findings, while behavioural economists such as Rabin defend them.

definition.text: A situation, also called a social dilemma, in which everyone would be better off cooperating but people fail to because their individual interests pull against joint action.

facts.text: Trouble arises when too many members chase individual, immediate gain instead of the group's long-term interest.
Resource depletion and low voter turnout are both explained as social dilemmas.
Climate change, biodiversity loss and waste build-up can all be described as collective action problems.
Without regulation, people and firms tend to pick the easier, cheaper option rather than the one that cuts emissions or saves non-renewable resources.
Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action argued that rational individuals do not automatically make a rational group.
Olson argued that for a pure public good, one contributor tends to give less as others give more.
It is analysed with game theory and the free-rider problem that arises in providing public goods.
David Hume described the problem in 1738 through neighbours agreeing to drain a meadow.

title: Solutions to social dilemmas
article: Collective action problem#Factors promoting cooperation in social dilemmas

definition.text: The three broad ways of getting people to cooperate in a social dilemma: motivational, strategic and structural solutions.

facts.text: Motivational solutions assume people care about others; research finds people have stable preferences for how much they weigh others' outcomes against their own.
Strategic solutions include tit for tat in repeated interactions: cooperate first, then copy the partner's last move.
Structural solutions change the rules of the game or remove the dilemma; monetary rewards have cut household water and electricity use.
Cooperation is more likely when people can monitor, sanction defectors, communicate, know one another and manage resources with clear boundaries.
Sanction systems are costly and are themselves public goods, and rewards can crowd out people's voluntary cooperation.
Graduated sanctions, which start mild and let violators regain trust, support collective resource management.

title: Endowment effect

definition.text: The finding that people value something more once they own it, so they are more likely to keep an object than to acquire the same object.

facts.text: People's maximum willingness to pay for an item is typically lower than the least they will accept to give it up, even for something owned only minutes.
In the classic Cornell mug study, owners asked about twice as much to sell a mug as buyers would pay for it.
Richard Thaler coined the term in 1980.
The leading explanation is loss aversion: giving up an owned item feels like a loss.
It contradicts the standard theory that willingness to pay and willingness to accept should be equal, and it undermines the Coase theorem.
Hanemann noted that the two need only be equal for close substitutes, so gaps for environmental resources and health can arise without an endowment effect.
Shogren and colleagues found little effect for goods with substitutes but accepted it for goods without them, such as non-renewable Earth resources.
Businesses exploit it with free trials, which give consumers a sense of ownership that makes them reluctant to cancel.

contested_note: Some economists question whether the effect exists, arguing it reflects lack of substitutes or artificial experimental scarcity.

definition.text: The branch of applied mathematics that models interactions between several decision-makers as games of strategy between players.

facts.text: It describes, predicts and evaluates choices, often assuming each player tries to maximise their payoff.
A game captures the choices available to each player and the payoffs that result.
A game is cooperative if players can make binding, externally enforced commitments, and non-cooperative if agreements must enforce themselves.
Players are usually assumed to be rational, with consistent preferences and unlimited capacity to calculate the best payoff.
In a Nash equilibrium each player's choice is a best response to the others, so no one gains by changing alone.
The field began with von Neumann and Morgenstern's 1944 book Theory of Games and Economic Behavior.
John Nash, John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten won the 1994 Nobel prize in economics for pioneering game theory.
It is a major method in economics for modelling competing agents, and is also used in biology, political science and the study of vaccination decisions.

definition.text: An economic experiment in which one player proposes how to split a sum of money and the other can accept, or reject so that both get nothing.

facts.text: It has become a popular tool of economic experiments, first described by John Harsanyi in 1961.
It shows how fairness, generosity and social acceptance shape players' decisions.

definition.text: An experiment that measures trust: an investor sends money to a trustee, the amount is tripled, and the trustee decides how much to return.

facts.text: It was designed by Berg, Dickhaut and McCabe in 1995.
A purely self-interested trustee would return nothing, but in experiments people do place trust, expecting reciprocity.

title: Loss aversion

definition.text: A bias in which the same situation feels worse when it is framed as a loss than when it is framed as a gain.

facts.text: Empirically, a loss tends to be treated as about twice as large as an equal gain.
Kahneman and Tversky coined the term in 1979 as part of prospect theory.
It differs from risk aversion, which is the rational valuing of an uncertain outcome below its expected value.
Losses are measured against a reference point, such as what a person already owns.
It was first proposed as the explanation for the endowment effect, and the two together break the Coase theorem.
Framing the same price change as a $5 discount or as a $5 surcharge avoided changes consumer behaviour significantly.
Expectations can also set the reference point, so missing an expected purchase feels like a loss.
One explanation is evolutionary: for an organism near the edge of survival, losing a day's food could be fatal while an extra day's food adds little.

contested_note: Several studies find no loss aversion under risk or at small stakes, and Gal argues psychological inertia explains the same findings.

definition.text: The tendency to pay more attention to a task when it involves losses, without giving losses more weight than gains.

facts.text: Eldad Yechiam and Guy Hochman proposed it as distinct from loss aversion.
Under loss attention, losses can reduce bias rather than cause it.
People pick options with higher expected value more often when outcomes are framed as losses.

definition.text: A thought experiment in which two players can each cooperate for mutual benefit or betray the other for individual gain.

facts.text: Betraying is the rational choice for each player, yet both would get a higher payoff by cooperating.
Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher designed the puzzle in 1950 at the RAND Corporation.
It is the basic game behind research on social dilemmas, showing how individual interests can conflict with the group's.
Climate change fits it: every country gains from a stable climate, but each hesitates to cut its own CO2 emissions.
Unlike the textbook game, climate politics has uncertain payoffs, which suggests states will cooperate even less.
Hardin's tragedy of the commons can be seen as a many-player version, in which widespread defection destroys the commons.
It has been called the E. coli of social psychology, used to study topics such as oligopoly and collective action.

definition.text: The prisoner's dilemma played repeatedly, with players remembering past moves and able to change strategy.

facts.text: It underlies some theories of human cooperation and trust.
If both players know the number of rounds is fixed, the equilibrium is to defect in every round.
In Robert Axelrod's 1984 computer tournaments, greedy strategies did poorly over time and more altruistic ones did better.
The winner was tit for tat: cooperate first, then copy the opponent's previous move.

title: Anchoring effect

definition.text: The tendency for judgments to be pulled toward a reference point, or anchor, even one that is completely irrelevant.

facts.text: Tversky and Kahneman described anchoring in 1974 as a heuristic for estimating under uncertainty.
People asked to estimate 1 x 2 x ... x 8 quickly gave a median of 512; those shown 8 x 7 x ... x 1 gave 2,250.
The usual explanation is that people adjust away from the anchor too little.
Anchoring is hard to avoid: even obviously wrong anchors about Gandhi's age at death shifted guesses to averages of 50 versus 67.
It appears in legal sentencing, shopping, salary negotiations and forecasting, and even experts are susceptible.
In negotiation, the first price offer sets the anchor for what follows.

contested_note: Scholars agree anchoring is easy to demonstrate but do not agree on what causes it.

definition.text: A shift in preference between two options when a third, usually inferior, option is added.

facts.text: The decoy might cost more than one option while being lower in quality than the other.
Restaurants pricing meal components separately next to a set meal use the decoy to raise willingness to pay for the set.
Decoy effects show individual irrationality that violates a standard axiom of choice.

title: Availability heuristic

definition.text: A mental shortcut that judges how likely or important something is by how easily examples come to mind.

facts.text: The easier the consequences of something are to recall, the bigger they tend to seem.
Tversky and Kahneman first studied and named it in 1973.
Wide media coverage of rare, vivid events such as homicides or airline accidents makes people overrate them compared with common diseases or car accidents.
Because recall is affected by more than real frequency, relying on it produces systematic biases.

contested_note: Critics argue that ease of recall, not the number of examples recalled, drives the effect, and that the classic studies are too vague about mental processes.

title: Bounded rationality in environmental decision making
article: Bounded rationality in environmental decision making

definition.text: The application of bounded rationality to how environmental policy decisions are made.

facts.text: Established environmental policy theory assumes homo economicus: fully rational, self-regarding people.
That assumption is troublesome because policymakers often have only an incomplete picture of an environmental problem.
All environmental actors are human, with limited cognitive abilities and incomplete information.
The more actors involved in an environmental decision, the more complex it becomes and the less predictable its outcome.
A green strategy, in line with the Porter hypothesis, uses strict rules expected to spur cleaner innovation; eco-dumping weakens rules to boost resource exports.
These two extremes try to solve many-sided wicked problems with one-sided policies.

title: Choice architecture

definition.text: The design of the ways choices are presented to people, and the effect that presentation has on what they decide.

facts.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein coined the term in their 2008 book Nudge.
Advocates use it to nudge people toward saving for retirement, healthier food or organ donation, compensating for decision biases.
Its tools include defaults, expecting error, feedback, structuring complex choices and incentives.
It can translate metrics into what people care about, such as turning energy use into greenhouse gas emissions.
It led to the UK's Behavioural Insights Team and a White House Nudge Unit.
Critics say it can limit choice, undermine autonomy, or raise firm profits at consumers' expense through dark patterns.
Responses differ by person; liberals and conservatives react differently to information about the environmental effects of energy use.

contested_note: Critics of libertarian paternalism argue choice architecture can impose costs on rational people and undermine autonomy, while its advocates say no presentation is neutral.

definition.text: The finding that offering many options can lower people's motivation to choose and their satisfaction with the choice.

facts.text: Classical economics predicts more options leave people at least as well off, but each option costs time and effort to evaluate.
How much it matters varies a lot between situations.
Choice architects can limit options or give decision support tools, though limiting options can reduce welfare.

title: Construal level theory

definition.text: A social-psychology theory that the more psychologically distant something is, the more abstractly people think about it, and the closer it is, the more concretely.

facts.text: The main kinds of psychological distance are distance in time, in space, in social terms, and in how likely an event is.
Nira Liberman and Yaacov Trope developed the theory.
Trope and Liberman argue it offers a framework for understanding time discounting, the lower value placed on future outcomes.
Psychological distance leads people to discount future risks and focus on immediate daily concerns, a barrier to pro-environmental behaviour.

contested_note: Social psychologists debate whether further dimensions of distance, such as informational or experiential distance, belong in the theory.

definition.text: The tendency for people to accept whatever option they get if they make no active choice.

facts.text: Experiments and observational studies show that making an option the default makes it more likely to be chosen.
Differences between opt-in and opt-out organ donor rules have been argued to be the main cause of large differences in donor rates between countries.
More consumers chose renewable electricity when it was offered as the default.
Explanations include the mental effort of choosing, switching costs, loss aversion relative to the default, and reading the default as a recommendation.
Defaults can be mass defaults applied to everyone or personalised defaults tailored to each customer.
Setting defaults is a key example of a nudge or soft paternalist policy.

title: Dictator game

definition.text: An economic experiment in which one player, the dictator, decides how to split a sum of money with a passive second player.

facts.text: It is a simplified version of the ultimatum game: the recipient cannot reject the offer.
Most dictators send some money, which shows the role of fairness and norms and undermines the assumption of narrow self-interest.
A wide cross-cultural study by Henrich and colleagues found dictators give a non-zero share everywhere.
Removing full anonymity raised giving from 18.3% to 27.2%, and dictators give less when they feel they earned the money.

contested_note: Some authors argue giving reflects a wish not to look greedy rather than altruism, and tests of this idea give mixed results.

definition.text: The difference between the cost-minimising level of energy efficiency and the level people and firms actually achieve.

facts.text: Its existence suggests society passes up cost-effective investments that could cut energy use at low cost.
Eric Hirst and Marilyn Brown coined the term in a 1990 paper.
Hirst and Brown split its causes into structural barriers, such as fuel prices that leave out social and environmental costs, and behavioural barriers in users' decisions.
High up-front costs, high discount rates, uncertain fuel prices and lack of information all hold back efficiency investments.
Jaffe and Stavins attribute it to both market failures, such as imperfect information, and non-market failures such as consumer inertia.
Remedies include subsidies and cheap loans, minimum building and equipment standards, information and labelling programmes, and government procurement.
It implies society forgoes cost-effective efficiency investments that could cut energy use substantially.
It exists because of market failures: fuel prices leave out social and environmental costs, future prices are uncertain, and upfront costs and capital limits deter buyers.

title: Field experiment

definition.text: An experiment carried out in a real-world setting rather than a laboratory.

facts.text: Researchers randomly assign subjects to treatment or control groups so that later differences reflect the treatment, not pre-existing differences.
Unlike natural experiments, the researchers themselves control the randomisation and how the treatment is delivered.
They offer higher external validity and can test people who do not know they are being studied.
Economists use them to study discrimination, health programmes, charitable fundraising, education and microfinance.
Spillovers to untreated groups, noncompliance and attrition can bias results, and they can be costly, hard to replicate and ethically fraught.
Behavioural economists turned to field studies partly in response to criticism of lab experiments.

notes: S:95303bb18578 on this page attributes the Stanford Prison Experiment to Stanley Milgram; not cited here, flag for verification.

definition.text: A bias in which people's choices change with the way the same options are worded, even when the options are logically identical.

facts.text: When choices are worded as gains, most people prefer a sure gain to a chance of gain; worded as losses, people tend to pick a gamble over a sure loss.
In Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 disease problem, a sure treatment was chosen by 72% when described as saving 200 lives, but 78% chose the risky one when outcomes were described as deaths.
Standard logic says a decision should not depend on how the problem is described; deciding on such irrelevant wording is called an extensionality violation.
93% of PhD students registered early when a late penalty fee was stressed, but only 67% when the same terms were shown as an early discount.
Framing shapes decisions in public health, education, politics, law and economics, and is counted among the largest biases in decision making.
People are more open to framing when they rely on fast, intuitive thinking rather than slow, deliberate thinking.
The effect seems to weaken when a decision is made in a foreign language, perhaps because it brings more distance and deliberation.
Valuation surveys of environmental goods have been criticised for bringing in framing effects.

definition.text: Mental shortcuts people use to reach judgments and decisions quickly.

facts.text: Humans, animals, organizations and even machines use simple strategies to form judgments and solve complex problems fast.
Heuristic answers are good enough for a pressing need when information is incomplete, but they are not always right and can differ from what logic and probability give.
Herbert A. Simon introduced the idea in the 1950s, and his satisficing rule was one of the first models of a heuristic.
In the 1970s Tversky and Kahneman linked heuristics to cognitive bias, first proposing availability, representativeness, and anchoring and adjustment.
Theories differ on whether heuristics are irrational: one view treats them as unavoidable shortcuts for a limited brain, another as fast methods that do as well as complex ones with less information.
In a computer test of ten simple decision rules, most picked the option with the highest expected value and almost never the lowest.

definition.text: Judging how likely something is by how closely it resembles a typical member of a category.

facts.text: It attends to an individual's traits while ignoring how common each category is in the population, which leads to the base rate fallacy.
Asked about a woman named Linda, people rated 'bank teller and active feminist' as likelier than 'bank teller', though a combination can never be more probable than one part of it.
Tversky and Kahneman argued it underlies the gambler's fallacy, the expectation that random outcomes even out over the short run.

definition.text: An unnoticed mental process in which a hard question is answered by replacing it with an easier, related one.

facts.text: Daniel Kahneman and Shane Frederick proposed it in 2002.
It explains why people can be unaware of their own biases and why biases persist even after people are told about them.
In the bat-and-ball puzzle many people wrongly answer $0.10, splitting $1.10 into a big and a small amount instead of working out the sum.
Travellers paid more for insurance against death in a terrorist attack than for insurance covering death of any kind, as fear stood in for a judgment of total risk.

definition.text: The view, argued by Gerd Gigerenzer and colleagues, that simple rules of thumb can give judgments as accurate as complicated procedures.

facts.text: This approach holds that heuristics perform as well as complex methods, but faster and with less information.
A fast-and-frugal tree makes a classification, such as whether chest pain signals a heart attack, by asking a short sequence of questions on few cues.
Some theories argue that a heuristic can be more accurate than weighing every known factor, the so-called less-is-more effect.

definition.text: The tendency to keep putting resources into a failing course of action in the hope of turning losses around.

facts.text: It arises when organisations or nations must decide whether to continue an operation or withdraw from it.
It is especially likely when the decision maker can claim credit for success while others absorb the losses.

definition.text: The 'economic man' of economic models: a picture of people as always rational and narrowly self-interested, pursuing their own goals in the best possible way.

facts.text: The model assumes people maximize their satisfaction (utility) as consumers and profit as producers, and can think through every possible outcome to pick the best.
Its 'rationality' only means reaching one's own goals at least cost; it does not judge whether those goals are rational in an ethical or social sense.
The term 'economic man' was first used in the late nineteenth century by critics of John Stuart Mill's political economy.
Adam Smith wrote that we expect our dinner not from the butcher's or baker's kindness but from their regard to their own interest.
It contrasts with behavioral economics, which studies biases, and with bounded rationality, which stresses limits of mind and time.
Its preferences need not be selfish: a person's utility can include the wellbeing of family members, which fits models that stress cooperation.
Advanced economic theory now uses modified models, such as agents with bounded rationality or envy, to depict real decisions more realistically.

definition.text: Arguments from economists, psychologists, anthropologists, sociologists and feminist scholars that the purely rational, self-interested model of people is unrealistic or one-sided.

facts.text: Economists such as Veblen, Keynes and Simon stressed uncertainty and bounded rationality, arguing perfect knowledge never exists.
Anthropologists found that in traditional societies production and exchange follow patterns of reciprocity, called a gift economy, rather than the model's predictions.
Bruno Frey criticised its stress on outside rewards and punishments over intrinsic motivation.
Feminist economists argue it undervalues unpaid care work such as caregiving and domestic labour.

definition.text: The idea that institutions can legitimately steer people's behavior for their own good while still leaving them free to choose otherwise.

facts.text: Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein coined the term in 2003 and defended it in their 2008 book Nudge.
It is libertarian because people can opt out of the arrangements, which is said to preserve freedom of choice.
Setting a default to exploit the default effect is a typical example.
Austria, with an opt-out organ donation system, has a consent rate of 99.98%, while Germany, with an opt-in system, has only 12%.
Firms that raised the default contribution rate of retirement plans immediately and sharply raised how much their employees saved.
Critics say it neglects the traditional libertarian concern with coercion and that other aims, such as future liberty, could be promoted instead.

definition.text: Richard Thaler's model of how people sort, label and judge money and economic outcomes in separate mental 'accounts'.

facts.text: People budget money into accounts such as saving for a home or spending on gas, clothing and utilities, partly to control their spending.
A person may stop eating out when that budget runs out but keep buying groceries, even though both come from the same income.
Thaler found people more willing to drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 purchase than on a $125 purchase.
It draws on prospect theory, and can make people more loss averse for some accounts than others, a systematic departure from rational consumer behaviour.
People are willing to pay more with credit cards than with cash, because the payment comes later and looks like a small addition to a large bill.
Households spend SNAP food benefits on food at a rate of 0.5 to 0.6 per dollar, much higher than the usual 0.1 from cash transfers.
Publicly setting a savings goal greatly raised savings rates in a study of savings groups in Colombia.

definition.text: The unpleasant feeling people get when they spend money, treated as a negative response to a financial loss.

facts.text: Typical examples are watching a taxi meter or a gas pump climb.
A $30 t-shirt feels like a bigger expense paid from $50 in a wallet than from $500 in a checking account.
Consumers who feel more pain of paying for the same goods hold less debt.

title: Motivation crowding theory

definition.text: The theory that outside rewards for a behavior, such as payment for a task, can sometimes weaken people's inner motivation to do it.

facts.text: Against the predictions of standard economics, the lowered motivation can reduce total performance.
Richard Titmuss argued in 1970 that paying for some behaviors could reduce them; Bruno Frey coined the term 'crowding out' in 1997.
In Edward Deci's classic study, people paid per puzzle solved did fewer unpaid puzzles in free time and reported less interest than people paid just for showing up.
Paying people a token amount to collect money for charity led them to collect less than unpaid volunteers.
Crowding out has been found in teachers' performance pay, commission pay, charitable giving and student performance, prompting calls to rethink incentives for volunteers.
Rewards seen as controlling are argued to replace inner motivation, while rewards seen as a mark of status or achievement can raise effort without crowding it out.
Crowding out is stronger when the reward is publicly known, since people who care about appearing altruistic avoid looking paid.
A 2020 review of over 100 tests found that paying for enjoyable tasks boosts performance, but removing an expected payment can leave people worse than if never paid.

contested_note: Some meta-analyses found mixed or null effects of rewards on inner motivation, while others found a robust effect for certain rewards once moderating factors are controlled.

definition.text: The tendency to take a smaller reward now rather than wait for a larger one later.

facts.text: It means overvaluing immediate rewards and giving too little weight to long-term consequences.
Early models assumed people discount the future at a steady rate, but research showed they discount sharply over short delays and less over longer ones, so their preferences are time-inconsistent.
Phelps and Pollak introduced the quasi-hyperbolic discounting model in 1968 to capture this.
Present-biased preferences often lead to procrastination, especially when actions bring immediate costs.
It discourages unpleasant actions for health, such as dieting, quitting smoking or regular check-ups, whose benefits come only later.
It is linked to strong desires to spend money and failure to stick to a saving plan.
Short-termism has been linked to present bias, which favours short-term payoffs over long-term rewards.

definition.text: The ability to resist an immediate reward in order to gain a more valuable reward later.

facts.text: In the Stanford marshmallow experiments, begun by Walter Mischel and Ebbe B. Ebbesen in 1970, children were promised a second treat if they waited about 15 minutes without eating the first.
Older children were better at waiting, and the ability to wait as a child correlated with success in follow-up studies years later.
People who are more patient about future political change are more willing to vote in elections.

definition.text: A theory of how people actually make choices under risk, developed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky in 1979.

facts.text: Unlike expected utility theory, which models what perfectly rational agents would do, it aims to describe real behavior.
People judge gains and losses relative to a reference point, their current situation, rather than by absolute wealth.
Losses are felt more sharply than equal gains: for some people the pain of losing $1,000 is only made up by the pleasure of gaining $2,000.
Its value function is concave for gains, convex for losses and steeper for losses, so people avoid risk over gains and seek risk over losses.
Choices pass through an editing phase, where a reference point is set and outcomes are coded as gains or losses, before they are evaluated.
It was cited when Kahneman received the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, and Tversky and Kahneman's work largely launched behavioral economics.
Jeffrey Berejikian used it to analyse how the Montreal Protocol, a landmark environmental agreement, came about.
Critics note that the reference point is hard to pin down, since many outside factors shape what counts as a gain or a loss.

definition.text: The tendency, derived from prospect theory, to focus on short-term gains and losses and weigh them more heavily than long-term ones.

facts.text: It can lead people to avoid immediate losses at the expense of long-term gains.
In a 1997 betting study by Gneezy and Potters, players bet more after losing a round and less after winning one, rather than looking at total earnings.

definition.text: A revised version of prospect theory that weights probabilities by rank, fixing flaws in the original version.

facts.text: The original version could prefer one prospect over another even when the other was at least as good at every outcome level, violating first-order stochastic dominance.
The cumulative version borrows its probability weighting from rank-dependent expected utility theory and also works for continuous outcomes.

definition.text: A standard economics experiment in which players secretly decide how many of their tokens to put into a shared pot that is multiplied and split among everyone.

facts.text: Each player's payoff is what they kept plus their share of the multiplied pot, so it is used to study altruism, cooperation and free riding.
If players are purely selfish, the Nash equilibrium is that nobody contributes.
It tests the theory that public goods, such as street lighting that no one can be excluded from, are under-provided because no one has a private motive to pay.
In repeated play contributions usually decline as generous players see others give less, but they rarely reach zero because a hard core of givers remains.
Players will punish non-contributors even at a cost to themselves, and in most experiments this raises group cooperation.
With 40 players, a multiplier of 1.03 leads almost everyone to stop giving, while a multiplier of 1.3 keeps average contributions around 50%.
Framing the same game as a climate negotiation rather than neutrally can change how players behave.
Contributions tend to be lower when players start with unequal endowments.

definition.text: A decision strategy of looking through options until one is good enough, rather than searching for the very best.

facts.text: Herbert A. Simon introduced the word, a blend of 'satisfy' and 'suffice', in 1956, though the idea first appeared in his 1947 book Administrative Behavior.
Simon used it for problems where the best answer cannot be found because the calculation is too hard or information is lacking.
A satisficer sets an aspiration level, takes the first option that meets it, and lowers the level if nothing meets it in time.
Of 628 used-car dealers studied, 97% used a form of satisficing, typically cutting a car's price by about 3% if it was unsold after 24 days.
The behavioral theory of the firm treats profit as a level to reach rather than something to maximize, after which firms pursue other goals.
Maximizers search more options than satisficers, yet tend to be less happy and more regretful about their choices.

definition.text: Jon Krosnick's theory that survey respondents cut down the mental effort of answering well by giving merely acceptable answers.

facts.text: In weak satisficing respondents go through every step but less thoroughly; in strong satisficing they give plausible answers without searching memory at all.
It shows up as 'don't know' answers, giving the same rating to every item, agreeing with any statement, or picking the first reasonable option.
It is more likely when respondents have less ability or motivation and when the task is hard.

definition.text: A standard of acceptable behavior shared by a group.

facts.text: Norms can be informal understandings or be written into rules and laws, and institutions are made up of many norms.
Unlike private ideas, attitudes or values, norms are shared beliefs about behavior, and they depend on context, group and history.
Many norms evolve without top-down design, through repeated interactions between individuals.
Breaking an informal norm brings reprimands, warnings or exclusion rather than legal penalties, and people who break norms are labelled deviants.
A norm's life cycle runs from emergence, pushed by norm entrepreneurs, to a cascade of broad acceptance, to internalization, when it is taken for granted.
Game theory can treat a norm as a rule of thumb that a rational person follows only when it benefits them, often modelled with a repeated game.
Social norms affect free riding on voluntarily provided public goods, an effect economic models often underestimate.

definition.text: Two kinds of social norm: descriptive norms show what people commonly do, while injunctive norms say what people ought to do.

facts.text: A parking lot with no litter on the ground signals the descriptive norm that most people there do not litter.
Seeing someone pick up trash and throw it away conveys the injunctive norm that one ought not to litter.
Voters in a US field experiment were more motivated to vote when told many people around them were voting, evidence that descriptive norms matter.

title: Social norms approach

definition.text: A campaign strategy, also called social norms marketing, that changes behavior by correcting people's mistaken beliefs about what their peers do.

facts.text: In the mid-1980s H.W. Perkins and A.D. Berkowitz found that college students greatly overestimated how much other students drank.
It rests on pluralistic ignorance: people wrongly believe others' attitudes or behavior differ from their own, often because extreme behavior is the most memorable.
Campaigns survey actual and perceived norms, broadcast messages such as 'Most students drink 0–4 drinks when they party', then evaluate and revise.
It has been used against smoking, drink driving and HIV risk, and to raise seat belt use.

contested_note: Some scholars question its assumptions and methods, and one nationwide study found no fall in drinking at colleges that used it.

definition.text: People's tendency to care not only about their own material payoff but also about others' payoffs and the intentions behind them.

facts.text: They include altruism, fairness, reciprocity and inequity aversion.
Research began with lab experiments around 1980, when players in games such as the ultimatum and dictator games departed systematically from pure self-interest.
In the ultimatum game proposers typically offer 25%-50% and responders tend to reject splits below 20%; in the dictator game the average gift falls to 20%, yet over 60% still give something.
Models divide them into distributive preferences, about how payoffs are shared, and reciprocal preferences, about the intentions behind others' actions.
Reciprocal and fairness-minded people can cooperate when they expect others to cooperate and can punish free riders, which matters for solving free-riding problems.
Kahneman, Knetsch and Thaler found that concern for fairness restrains firms from, for example, raising prices after demand rises.
Without such preferences, society would be unlikely to reach desirable allocations because of self-interest and free riding.

definition.text: The motivation to answer kind behavior with kindness and unfair behavior with unkindness.

facts.text: Rabin's 1993 model, one of the earliest, has people judge another's kindness by comparing what they receive with a fair payoff.
In the trust game, first movers typically pass on about 50% of their endowment, and the amount returned grows with the amount sent.
Reciprocal altruism may evolve from expecting future kindness in return; tit-for-tat in the prisoner's dilemma is an example.

definition.text: A bias toward keeping things as they currently are, also called default bias.

facts.text: The current state serves as a reference point, so any change from it is felt as a loss or a gain.
It is explained by loss aversion and the endowment effect: the possible losses of switching weigh more than the possible gains.
It differs from a rational preference for the status quo, where the current state really is better, and from simple inertia.
Samuelson and Zeckhauser showed in 1988 that people stick with an option framed as the status quo, and that the pull grows as more alternatives are offered.
In a 1986 retirement study, most people never changed how they split savings between two funds, despite very different returns and no switching costs.
Automatic enrolment in retirement plans, where employees must opt out, uses this bias to raise saving.
Defaults keep their effect even when people are told why the default was chosen.

definition.text: A check for status quo bias: if changing a quantity one way is judged bad, ask whether changing it the other way is also judged bad.

facts.text: If both directions are judged bad, those judging must explain why the current value cannot be improved; if they cannot, status quo bias is suspected.
Its rationale is that of all possible values only a few can be best, so it is unlikely that the current value happens to be one of them.

definition.text: An economic theory of the emotional reward people get from giving to others.

facts.text: In James Andreoni's original model (1989, 1990), people enjoy 'doing their part' whatever the actual impact of their gift.
It describes impure altruism, a mix of altruistic and selfish motives for giving.
Under pure altruism, government grants should fully crowd out private donations; warm glow helps explain why they do not.

Because outside rewards and punishments have often failed to bring lasting green behavior, environmental policy increasingly targets warm glow, with promising results for green energy, recycling and carpooling.
Sustainable investors may get satisfaction from the act itself rather than its impact, so their utility does not rise in line with impact.
A meta-analysis of 36 brain-imaging studies found the brain's reward networks consistently active when people choose to give.
Andreoni himself called adding warm glow to the model 'an admittedly ad hoc fix'.

title: Pro-environmental behavior

definition.text: Behaviour people consciously choose to reduce the harm their actions do to the environment.

facts.text: Green consumption, buying in ways that harm the environment as little as possible, is one form of it.
Money incentives, costs, regulations and policy norms, along with how much time, money and power people feel they have, shape it through their attitudes.
Barriers to it can be psychological, social or cultural, financial, or structural, such as a home location that forces car dependency.
A meta-analysis confirmed a strong correlation between nature connectedness and pro-environmental behaviour, but found a weaker causal role than assumed.
Climate change narratives told as stories were better at inspiring it in a 2019 study.
Environmental psychology studies the psychological factors behind it and how to encourage it to mitigate climate change and biodiversity loss.

notes: Phrase concept; the page Barriers to pro-environmental behaviour (crawled, another chapter) supplies the definition.
